section_titles: Equal sharing and the concept of half
periods.activity_title: Folding to Find the Fair Half

tasks_in_class.description: How do you share objects equally?
Why is Shabnam folding the paratha over itself?
Circle the shapes where half of the whole is coloured.
Draw a line to show one-half of the whole.
Take a rectangular sheet of paper and fold it in half. Find all the different ways to make a half. Repeat with a square piece of paper.

time_bands.activity: Open with Let us Discuss Q1, p.107 ("How do you share objects equally?") — children suggest ideas aloud and the class tests each suggestion against the fairness question: does everyone get the same?

Move to Let us Discuss Q2, p.107 ("Why is Shabnam folding the paratha over itself?") — each child folds a paper square to mirror the paratha-fold, presses the two halves together, and articulates to a partner why the fold proves equal shares.
Children work on Let us Do Q1, p.108 ("Circle the shapes where half of the whole is coloured.") — after individual work, pairs compare circled choices and reason aloud about any disagreements.
Children complete Let us Do Q2, p.108 ("Draw a line to show one-half of the whole.") — each then shares one drawing and the class checks whether the line produces two matching parts.

Hands-on exploration: Let us Explore, p.110 ("Take a rectangular sheet of paper and fold it in half…") — children fold rectangular then square sheets in as many ways as they can discover, noting each new fold on the sheet.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often think 'half' simply means 'cut somewhere in the middle' rather than two equal parts — press the fold-and-overlay test each time a child offers a new line. Additional pictorial tasks are in Let us Do Q3–Q6 (pp.109–110) and Let us Do p.110, which the teacher may assign as further practice or homework. Carry the paper-folding discovery into the next concept by naming it: 'We found that a half always means two parts that match exactly.'
materials: Square and rectangular paper sheets (one each per child)

section_titles: Equal sharing and the concept of half

tasks_in_class.description: Shabnam has eaten some chikki from 3 sides. Tick how much chikki is left: (a) less than half (b) more than half (c) half.
Draw lines to show different ways of making a half.
Complete the whole picture by drawing the other half.
Is Amit's way of sharing the mango tree, solar lamp, and woollen blanket fair? Is there another fair way?

time_bands.activity: Children examine Let us Do Q3, p.109 ("Shabnam has eaten some chikki from 3 sides. Tick how much chikki is left…") — they compare the remaining piece to an imagined half and justify their tick to a partner.

Open exploration: Let us Do Q5, p.109 ("Draw lines to show different ways of making a half.") — children try to find as many different dividing lines as they can; the class collects their answers on the board to build a shared record of possibilities.

Pictorial reconstruction: Let us Do Q6, p.109 ("Complete the whole picture by drawing the other half.") — children fold their paper along the printed half-line to check symmetry before finalising their drawing.

Discussion: Let us Discuss, p.110 ("Is Amit's way of sharing the mango tree, solar lamp, and woollen blanket fair?") — small groups of three debate each object and propose alternative fair shares; one group spokesperson states the fairest solution for each.

periods.teacher_notes: The paper-folding children used to verify equal halves is the same check to apply here: if you fold the remaining chikki piece, do both layers match? Students frequently confuse 'same shape' with 'same size' when completing the mirror drawing — prompt them to fold and overlay. Let us Do Q4, p.109 ("Show by colouring half a chikki eaten from 2 sides") is available as additional practice at the teacher's discretion.
materials: Small square paper pieces for folding check

periods.activity_title: Marble Counts — Half and Double on the Line

tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks: 4 marbles are ___ of 8; 8 marbles are ___ of 4; 10 marbles are ___ of 5; 5 marbles are ___ of 10; 6 marbles are ___ of 12; 12 marbles are ___ of 6.
On a number line, how far is 13 from the double of 7? How far is 5 from half of 14?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Guess Who am I? Q1, p.112
tasks_in_class.description: I have less than the double of 3 marbles and more than the half of 8 marbles. Tick the correct answer from (a) 4, (b) 5, (c) 6 marbles.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Guess Who am I? Q2, p.112
tasks_in_class.description: I have less than the double of 4 marbles and more than the half of 10 marbles. Tick the correct answer from (a) 8, (b) 6, (c) 3 marbles.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the marble scenario from p.111: pairs count out small groups of counters and check whether one count is exactly half or double the other, before working through Fill in blanks, p.111 ("Fill in the blanks: 4 marbles are ___ of 8…").

Number line work: Number line, p.111 ("On a number line, how far is 13 from the double of 7? How far is 5 from half of 14?") — children mark the relevant values on the printed number line, count the gap, and write a sentence naming the distance.

Puzzle: Guess Who am I? Q1, p.112 ("I have less than the double of 3… and more than the half of 8…") — children compute each bound, locate both on the number line, then identify which of the three options sits between them.

Puzzle: Guess Who am I? Q2, p.112 ("I have less than the double of 4… and more than the half of 10…") — same strategy; children compare their reasoning with a partner and explain why the other two options are ruled out.

periods.teacher_notes: The equal-halves concept children developed by folding — where half of a shape means two matching parts — extends here: half of a number means the pair that makes up the whole count. A common error is doubling instead of halving (and vice versa) when filling the blanks; encourage children to check by asking 'If I have two equal groups of this number, do I get the whole?' The number line is the anchor for the puzzle reasoning — children should mark the double and half before trying to choose.
materials: Small counters or pebbles (about 20 per pair)

periods.activity_title: Four Friends, One Chikki — Meeting the Quarter

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the objects that show quarters.
Draw lines to make a quarter of the whole (square, circle, flower, diamond).
Draw the remaining three quarters and complete the whole: (a) fan shape (b) striped rectangle.
Draw the remaining quarters to complete the whole: (a) chocolate bar quarter (b) L-shaped quarter.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the four-children chikki story from p.113: each child folds a square sheet first in half, then in half again, opens it out, and counts four equal parts — naming each part 'one quarter' aloud before opening the textbook.

Let us Do Q1, p.113 ("Tick the objects that show quarters.") — children circle each candidate, then explain to a partner how they know four equal parts are shown; the class discusses any disagreements.

Let us Do Q2, p.113 ("Draw lines to make a quarter of the whole — square, circle, flower, diamond.") — children draw two crossing lines and check that all four pieces look equal, folding paper models alongside when uncertain.

Reconstruction tasks: Let us Do Q3, p.113 ("Draw the remaining three quarters…") and Let us Do Q4, p.113 ("Draw the remaining quarters to complete the whole…") — children complete both and then compare finished wholes with a neighbour to verify.

periods.teacher_notes: The halving-by-folding children practised earlier is the direct bridge: fold in half, then fold that half again, and the result is a quarter. The most frequent error is drawing lines that create four pieces of unequal size and still calling them quarters — press children to fold and check overlap. Use the term 'one quarter' consistently and not '1 out of 4', following the section's language guidance.

section_titles: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
periods.activity_title: Building the Whole — One Quarter at a Time

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the appropriate word (half/a quarter/double) to complete sentences about Shabnam's and Lakshanya's coloured birds and tied flowers.
Tick the shapes below that show three-quarters.
Colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters, 4 quarters, 3 quarters, 1 quarter.
Here is a rectangle which shows quarters. Discuss how.

homework.description: Draw lines and colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters, 4 quarters, 3 quarters, 1 quarter.

time_bands.activity: Using the circle model on p.114, the class builds from 1 quarter to 4 quarters step by step — children hold up fingers for each added quarter and name aloud: 'two quarters is the same as a half, four quarters is a whole.'

Half or Quarter?, p.114 ("Tick the appropriate word — half/a quarter/double — to complete sentences about Shabnam's and Lakshanya's coloured birds and tied flowers.") — pairs discuss, then the class compares answers and explains each choice.
Let us Do Q1, p.115 ("Tick the shapes below that show three-quarters.") — children identify and justify; the teacher asks: 'How do you know it is three quarters and not two?'

Let us Do Q2, p.115 ("Colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters…") — children colour independently, then use the four-fold paper model to verify each shaded count.

Let us Do Q4, p.116 ("Here is a rectangle which shows quarters. Discuss how.") — a quick class discussion; children articulate why the rectangle's arrangement constitutes quarters even if the pieces differ in shape.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who grasped that four equal folds make four quarters can use that physical model to verify colouring tasks — press this habit. A common error is colouring any three sections for 'three quarters' without checking that all four sections are equal; the fold-and-check technique corrects this. Let us Do Q3, p.116 is set as an unhurried drawing task for home practice.

section_titles: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
periods.activity_title: Grid Explorations and the Fraction-Card Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Show quarters and halves in different ways in the grids given below.
Use the fraction cards from your book to form a whole.

time_bands.activity: Brief warm-up: children fold a square sheet into quarters, colour different counts, and call out the fraction name — connecting the colouring work on quarter-recognition to the open grid task ahead.

Let us Do Q5, p.116 ("Show quarters and halves in different ways in the grids given below.") — children shade grid squares in as many different patterns as they can to represent each named fraction, comparing approaches with a neighbour.

Let us Do Q6, p.116 ("Use the fraction cards from your book to form a whole.") — children cut the perforated fraction cards carefully, then try all combinations that build back to a complete whole, recording which sets work.
Closing share-out: two or three children hold up their card arrangements; the class names the fraction each card shows and verifies the total is one whole.

periods.teacher_notes: The grid task is deliberately open — children who found only two or three patterns should be encouraged to rotate or reflect their shading to find more, reinforcing the symmetry insight from the half-folding work. For the fraction-card puzzle, children often attempt to line up cards edge to edge without checking equal size; prompt them to overlay cards on the book's original shape to verify. Ensure scissors are available for the perforated sheet before the unit begins.
materials: Perforated fraction-card sheet from the book
Square paper and crayons for warm-up

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Here is a circle. Draw one straight line inside it to show two equal halves. How do you know the two parts are equal?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A diameter drawn through the centre of the circle; the two parts are equal because they match when you fold one on top of the other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw a line through the centre and check by folding — if both layers match, the parts are equal halves.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold the page along their line to check; stretch: ask them to draw a second, different diameter line and explain why that also shows halves.

exercise.description: Draw a line to show one-half of the whole.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt:
Look at the shape below. One half is drawn for you. Draw the other half to complete the whole shape.
[A simple L-shape printed on the left side of a vertical mirror line]

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A mirror-image L-shape drawn on the right side of the line, so that folding along the line makes both halves overlap exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reflect each point of the given half to the same distance on the opposite side of the dividing line.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold the paper along the mirror line and trace through; stretch: ask them to create their own shape and draw its mirror half for a partner to check.

exercise.description: Complete the whole picture by drawing the other half.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Priya folds a square piece of paper. Which of the following folds gives her two equal halves?

options.label: A
options.text: Fold from one corner to the opposite corner along the diagonal.

options.label: B
options.text: Fold anywhere across the middle so that the two flaps look roughly the same.

options.label: C
options.text: Fold a small strip along one edge of the square.

options.label: D
options.text: Fold from one corner to any point on the opposite side.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A diagonal fold of a square creates two equal right-angled triangles that match exactly when overlaid — this is a valid half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Overlay both layers after folding; if they match exactly in size and shape, the fold gives two equal halves.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child thinks 'looks roughly the same' is enough — they have not yet internalised the exact-match criterion for equal halves.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confuses any fold with a halving fold; they need to reconnect folding to the equal-parts definition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child thinks any line from a corner divides equally — they have not checked that the resulting pieces match.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically fold a paper square along each option and overlay the layers; stretch: ask whether the diagonal fold of a rectangle also gives equal halves and why.

exercise.description: Take a rectangular sheet of paper and fold it in half. Find all the different ways to make a half. Repeat with a square piece of paper.

items.prompt: Here is a square. Draw lines inside it to make four equal parts. Shade one part. What is that one shaded part called?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two lines crossing at the centre (one horizontal, one vertical) divide the square into four equal parts; one part shaded; the shaded part is called one quarter.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold in half, then fold in half again — the four equal parts each show one quarter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold a square paper twice and trace the fold lines onto the square in the book; stretch: ask them to shade three parts and name that fraction.

exercise.description: Draw lines to make a quarter of the whole (square, circle, flower, diamond).

items.prompt:
One quarter of a shape is drawn for you below. Draw the remaining three quarters to complete the whole shape.
[A small right-angled triangle representing one quarter of a square is given in the top-left corner of the square outline]

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three more right-angled triangles of the same size drawn to fill the remaining three-quarters of the square, completing it.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Repeat the given quarter piece three more times, rotating or reflecting as needed, until the whole square is filled with four matching parts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child cut out the given quarter from scrap paper and trace it three times into the shape; stretch: ask them to find a different way to divide the same square into four equal parts.

exercise.description: Draw the remaining quarters to complete the whole: (a) chocolate bar quarter (b) L-shaped quarter.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Here is a grid of 8 squares arranged in 2 rows of 4. Shade squares to show one quarter of the grid. Can you shade a different set of squares that also shows one quarter? Draw your second answer beside the first.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two squares shaded for the first answer (2 out of 8 = one quarter); a different pair of squares — any other 2 — shaded for the second answer.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: One quarter of 8 is 2 (since 4 quarters make the whole 8), so shade any 2 squares for each answer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to first count all 8 squares, then ask how many make one quarter if four equal groups fill the whole; stretch: ask them to show three quarters in yet another arrangement.

exercise.description: Show quarters and halves in different ways in the grids given below.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Rohan has four fraction cards. Each card shows one quarter of a circle. He wants to put them together to form one complete circle. How many cards does he need to use?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Four cards, because four quarters make one whole circle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count up quarters: 1 quarter + 1 quarter + 1 quarter + 1 quarter = 4 quarters = 1 whole.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child confuses quarters with halves — they think two pieces complete the whole.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may be thinking of three-quarters as the whole, not yet consolidating that four quarters equal one whole.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is doubling the number of quarters needed, possibly confusing this with a doubling rule from the half-and-double work.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold a paper circle twice and count the four equal parts before deciding; stretch: ask how many quarter cards would be needed to make two complete circles.

exercise.description: Use the fraction cards from your book to form a whole.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Meena cuts a chapati and gives one piece to her brother. Her brother says, 'This is not half!' How would you explain to Meena what she needs to do to make sure each piece is exactly half?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meena needs to fold the chapati over itself so that one part lies exactly on top of the other — if the edges and corners all match, each piece is one half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fold-and-overlay test: if both layers match completely, the two pieces are equal halves.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to act out the explanation using a square piece of paper; stretch: ask whether Meena could cut the chapati differently and still get two equal halves — what other cuts would work?

exercise.description: Why is Shabnam folding the paratha over itself?

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Look at the four shapes below. In which shape is exactly half of the whole coloured?

options.label: A
options.text: A rectangle with one small corner shaded

options.label: B
options.text: A circle with exactly the left half shaded, divided by a vertical diameter

options.label: C
options.text: A square with three of its four equal parts shaded

options.label: D
options.text: A triangle with a thin strip along one side shaded

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The circle divided by a diameter with exactly one side shaded — the shaded region and the unshaded region are equal, each being one half.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check that the shaded part and the unshaded part are equal in size; overlay or fold to confirm.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is not comparing the shaded and unshaded portions — they may think any shaded region counts as a half.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confuses three-quarters with a half — they have not yet secured the idea that half means two equal parts.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child is accepting any division as a half without checking whether the two parts are equal.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold a copy of each shape along the shading boundary and check for a match; stretch: ask them to re-draw one of the incorrect shapes so that it does show half.

exercise.description: Circle the shapes where half of the whole is coloured.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: A biscuit was whole. Someone ate a large piece from one side. Looking at what is left, which is the best description?

options.label: D
options.text: The whole biscuit is still there

teacher_guide.expected_answer: More than half is left — a large piece was eaten from one side, so the remaining piece is bigger than half of the original biscuit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the eaten piece to the remaining piece: if the eaten piece is clearly smaller, the remaining piece is more than half.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child is confusing the eaten portion with the remaining portion — they may think 'someone ate a lot' means 'very little is left.'
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child thinks any split of an object into two pieces is a half, regardless of whether they are equal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child has not processed that a piece was eaten — comprehension of the scenario needs support.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child physically tear a strip from one edge of a paper rectangle and hold both pieces side by side to compare size; stretch: ask them to describe where exactly the biscuit would need to be bitten so that exactly half is left.

exercise.description: Shabnam has eaten some chikki from 3 sides. Tick how much chikki is left: (a) less than half (b) more than half (c) half.

items.section_title: Equal sharing and the concept of half
items.prompt: Rajan says he will share a blanket fairly with his sister by using one end himself and giving the other end to her. His sister says this is not fair. Who is right, and why?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The sister is right. Sharing fairly means each person gets an equal part. Using 'one end' does not guarantee equal shares — the blanket must be folded so both halves match before dividing.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the equal-halves test: fold the blanket and check that both layers are the same size before saying the share is fair.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to act out the scenario with a sheet of paper, folding it to show what a fair share looks like; stretch: ask whether there is more than one fair way to divide a rectangular blanket in half.

exercise.description: Is Amit's way of sharing the mango tree, solar lamp, and woollen blanket fair? Is there another fair way?

items.prompt: Look at the number line below. Mark the double of 6 and the half of 16. Then write: how far apart are those two values?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Double of 6 = 12; half of 16 = 8. The distance between 12 and 8 is 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Double 6 by adding 6 to itself (6 + 6 = 12); halve 16 by splitting into two equal groups (16 ÷ 2 = 8); count the gap between 8 and 12 on the number line.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child count up from 6 twice on the number line to find the double, and count back from 16 in two equal jumps to find the half; stretch: ask what number is the double of the half of 16.

exercise.description: On a number line, how far is 13 from the double of 7? How far is 5 from half of 14?

items.prompt: I am a number. I am more than the half of 12, and I am less than the double of 5. Which number am I?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7. Half of 12 is 6; double of 5 is 10. The mystery number must be more than 6 and less than 10. Among the options, 7 is the only value in that range.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the lower bound (half of 12 = 6) and upper bound (double of 5 = 10), then check which option falls strictly between them.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have halved 12 incorrectly or confused the inequality direction — 4 is below the lower bound.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child chose the double of 5 itself rather than a number strictly less than it — they misread 'less than' as 'less than or equal to'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have chosen the larger number in the clue without computing either bound — comprehension of both constraints needs support.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child mark half of 12 and double of 5 on a number line, then circle numbers that lie between them; stretch: ask them to make up their own 'Guess Who am I?' clue using half and double that has exactly one correct answer.

exercise.book_ref: Guess Who am I? Q1, p.112
exercise.description: I have less than the double of 3 marbles and more than the half of 8 marbles. Tick the correct answer from (a) 4, (b) 5, (c) 6 marbles.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly shows one quarter of a shape?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with 1 part shaded.

options.label: B
options.text: A square divided into 2 equal parts with 1 part shaded.

options.label: C
options.text: A rectangle divided into 4 unequal parts with 1 part shaded.

options.label: D
options.text: A triangle divided into 3 equal parts with 1 part shaded.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A circle divided into 4 equal parts with 1 part shaded — this shows one quarter because the whole is split into four equal pieces and one is selected.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check that the whole is split into exactly four equal parts; one shaded equal part is one quarter.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child confuses a half (2 equal parts, 1 shaded) with a quarter — they have not yet connected the word 'quarter' to the count of four equal parts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child thinks any four parts constitute quarters — they have not yet applied the equal-size condition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child confuses one-third (3 equal parts, 1 shaded) with one quarter — they may need to count parts more carefully.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child fold paper into four equal parts and compare to each option; stretch: ask the child to explain why option C does not show a quarter even though it has four parts.

exercise.description: Tick the objects that show quarters.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Nitu has 12 flowers. She ties half of them into one bunch and gives a quarter of them to her friend. How many flowers does Nitu give to her friend?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 flowers. One quarter of 12 means 12 split into 4 equal groups; each group has 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 12 into 4 equal groups (12 ÷ 4 = 3); one group is one quarter.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child may have halved twice (12 → 6 → 3) but then halved again — or confused quarter with one-eighth.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child computed half of 12 rather than a quarter — they may be confusing the two operations.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may have guessed or applied a division by 3 — they need to connect 'quarter' to dividing into four equal parts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw 12 dots and circle them in four equal groups to find one group; stretch: ask how many flowers are in three quarters of 12.

exercise.description: Tick the appropriate word (half/a quarter/double) to complete sentences about Shabnam's and Lakshanya's coloured birds and tied flowers.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: Which of the following shapes shows three-quarters shaded?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle split into 4 equal parts, with 3 parts shaded.

options.label: B
options.text: A square split into 4 equal parts, with 1 part shaded.

options.label: C
options.text: A rectangle split into 4 equal parts, with 2 parts shaded.

options.label: D
options.text: A triangle split into 3 equal parts, with 3 parts shaded.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A circle split into 4 equal parts with 3 parts shaded shows three-quarters.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the total equal parts (must be 4) and the shaded parts (must be 3); both conditions together confirm three-quarters.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The child identifies four equal parts but selects one-quarter instead of three-quarters — they may not have read the question carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child selects two parts out of four, which is two-quarters (a half), not three-quarters — they may confuse these fractions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child sees all parts shaded and picks it, confusing a whole (3 out of 3) with three-quarters — they need to track both the denominator and numerator.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to fold a paper circle into four equal parts, shade three, and compare to the options; stretch: ask them to explain why option D is a whole, not three-quarters.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes below that show three-quarters.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: A rectangle is divided into four parts by two lines crossing inside it. Your friend says the four parts are quarters. How would you check whether your friend is right?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cut or fold the rectangle along both lines and check that all four pieces are the same size — if they match exactly, each part is one quarter. If the pieces differ, the parts are not quarters.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Overlay or fold each piece onto the others: equal size on all four means each is one quarter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw two crossing lines on a paper rectangle, cut the four pieces, and stack them to compare; stretch: ask them to draw a rectangle and a crossing that does NOT make quarters, and explain why.

exercise.description: Here is a rectangle which shows quarters. Discuss how.

items.prompt: Fill in the blank: 9 is the ___ of 18.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Half. 9 is the half of 18 because 9 + 9 = 18.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check: 9 + 9 = 18, so 9 is one of two equal groups that make 18 — it is the half.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child has reversed the relationship — they may think the larger number is always the double of the smaller when stated in this order.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The child confuses half with quarter — they need to reconnect 'half' to splitting into two equal parts, not four.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child may not yet see 9 as part of 18 at all — they may need to work with counters to group 18 into two equal sets.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to put out 18 counters and split them into two equal piles, then count each pile; stretch: ask them to write the related double sentence (9 doubled is 18) alongside.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks: 4 marbles are ___ of 8; 8 marbles are ___ of 4; 10 marbles are ___ of 5; 5 marbles are ___ of 10; 6 marbles are ___ of 12; 12 marbles are ___ of 6.

items.section_title: Quarters and Whole — building 1 to 4 quarters
items.prompt: A square is divided into 4 equal parts. Two parts are shaded. Which fraction does the shaded area show?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two quarters. Two out of four equal parts are shaded, which is two quarters (also equal to a half).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count shaded parts (2) out of total equal parts (4) to name the fraction: two quarters.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The child counted only one shaded part or confused 'two parts' with 'one quarter' — they need to count each shaded piece separately.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The child may have subtracted: 4 − 2 = 2, but then named the unshaded portion instead — they reversed which part to name.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The child chose four quarters (the whole) rather than counting only the shaded portion — they need to focus on the shaded parts only.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to fold a paper square into four equal parts and shade two, then count the shaded pieces aloud; stretch: ask them to colour a different shape to show two quarters and check whether it also looks like a half.

exercise.description: Colour the shapes below to show the fractions as instructed: 2 quarters, 1 quarter, 3 quarters, 4 quarters, 3 quarters, 1 quarter.
